paragraphs: I have often noticed that the Americans generally treat business in clear, plain language, free of any ornament and so extremely simple as to be often coarse. Yet they are apt to become inflated as soon as they attempt a more poetic diction. They then vent their pomposity from one end of a speech to the other. To hear them lavish imagery on every occasion, one might think they never spoke of anything simply. The English are more rarely given to a similar failing. The cause of this can be pointed out without much difficulty. In democratic communities each citizen is habitually occupied with contemplating a very puny object, namely himself. If he ever raises his eyes higher, he sees nothing but the immense form of society at large, or the still more imposing aspect of mankind. His ideas are either extremely small and clear, or extremely general and vague. What lies between is an open void. When he has been drawn out of his own sphere, therefore, he always expects some amazing object to be offered to his attention. Only on these terms does he consent to tear himself, for an instant, from the petty, complicated cares that form the charm and the excitement of his life. This seems to me enough to explain why men in democracies, whose concerns are in general so paltry, call on their poets for conceptions so vast and descriptions so unlimited.

The authors, for their part, do not fail to obey a tendency they share themselves. They perpetually inflate their imaginations and expand them beyond all bounds, and they not infrequently abandon the great in order to reach the gigantic. By these means they hope to attract the attention of the multitude and to fix it easily upon themselves. Nor are their hopes disappointed, for as the multitude looks for nothing in poetry but subjects of very vast dimensions, it has neither the time to measure accurately the proportions of all the subjects set before it, nor a taste correct enough to perceive at once in what respect they are out of proportion. The author and the public corrupt one another at the same time.

As we have just seen, the sources of poetry among democratic nations are grand but not abundant. They run dry quickly. Poets then cannot find the elements of the ideal in what is real and true, so they drop reality entirely and invent monsters. I am not afraid that the poetry of democratic nations will turn out too dull or hug the ground too closely. My fear is rather that it will keep losing itself in the clouds and will finally wander into purely imaginary regions. I fear that democratic poets’ works may often be crammed with immense and incoherent imagery, exaggerated descriptions, and strange creations, and that the fantastic beings of their imagination may sometimes make us long for the world of reality.
